Because it will be possible. It will be possible. We've already had the House because of Nancy Pelosi's leadership. Take up HR1, which is the most ambitious reform package passed by the House of Representatives since the Voting Rights Act of 1965. They've already done it. And if the Senate is taken over by Democrats, then even Charles Schumer would make sure that the Senate would pass at least HR1, as you'll hear in this podcast, maybe something better. So the focus on that day when the smoke of these current crises has passed will be what is going to happen in the first hundred days. And as you know, we've been fighting in the course of the last two years to build a movement at the presidential level first and now at the level of Congress to make sure that the first thing that happens in those first hundred days is the passage of fundamental reform to change the way our corrupted democracy functions. And that reform, as you've heard again and again, is money in politics, it's gerrymandering, it's equal access, equal freedom to vote, is to assure ethics inside of Congress, it's to assure the corrupting influence of money doesn't pervade every aspect of our government. It is to, let's coin a phrase, drain the swamp. That might be familiar to some of you. And so there is a chance we can do that. And the guests that I have the privilege of talking to today will be at the center of that discussion. Rokahana represents the 17th Congressional District in California. He's young. He's in his mid-40s. He's someone I've known for almost 20 years. In 2003, he wrote to me when I was the Director of the Stanford Center for Internet and Society and offered to volunteer to support the work of the center as a lawyer working in Silicon Valley. He ended up helping us launch Creative Commons by helping frame an understanding of the public domain and how the public domain could be supported by Creative Commons. In 2003, he had the insane idea of running for Congress against then incumbent Tom Lantosch. Tom Lantosch was an extraordinary figure. He was an immigrant from Hungary. He had been serving in Congress forever. And though he was of loyal, predictable, democratic vote, what was astonishing about Tom Landosh was that he had supported the president and the president's call to go to war in Iraq. And Rokahana was so committed to the mistake of that war that he wanted to run a campaign as a 20-something-year-old lawyer against this incredibly well-heeled and well-supported and well-loved member of Congress. I love insane ideas, so I was eager to help him, and we tried to push as hard as we could, but of course, he got crushed. And so then Roe worked as an IP lawyer. In 2009, he was appointed Deputy Assistant Secretary in the Department of Commerce, focusing on trade. After government, he went back to private practice. But in 2014, he again decided to take on an incumbent, this time Mike Honda. And he challenged Mike in the primary, and he lost, not by a lot. And then in 2016, he again challenged Miconda. And this time, surprising many, he won. And he has become a leader, a progressive voice and a leader for technology in Congress. He was an early supporter of AOC. And he has crafted a balance, really important, balanced approach to technological issues in the context of Congress. In 2018, he drafted something called the Internet Bill of Rights, which even Tim Berners-Lee, that's Sir Tim Berners-Lee, who the founder of the World Wide Web has endorsed. And he's been a leader carrying the importance of technology and innovation across the nation. But of course, our reason for talking to Roe is not all of these other extraordinary things that he's done, nor the extraordinary future that he will certainly have in politics in America. It is the question of reform. In 2017, Roe co-founded the No Pack Caucus in Congress. He founded that with two other members of Congress. One we've spoken to, Beto O'Rourke and the other Jared Polis, who is now the governor of Colorado. The three of them refused to take any contributions from political action committees. There are now three others who've joined their ranks. Phil Rowe, Francis Rooney, and someone else we've spoken to, John Sarbanes. He's been committed to the importance of reforming the corrupting influence of money and politics. And one of the reasons he is committed was that he and I share a common ancestry in our education, the scholar, Bruce Ackerman. And Bruce Ackerman, of course, with Ian Ayers, crafted the idea in a really robust way. It's an idea that had been bouncing around in the academic debates for many years, but he crafted it in a robust way to support what's called democracy dollars, or vouchers, which you've heard spoken of in this podcast again and again. And Roe introduced into Congress a plan to give every citizen $50 to spend in federal elections. This was before this current presidential election cycle. $50 seemed like a lot of money back then. Of course, since he did that, candidates like Andrew Yang proposed $100 vouchers. And then Kirsten Gillibrand proposed $200 per federal election, which means in some elections you could have $600 as vouchers to help fund campaigns differently. This is an idea that has really taken off and Roe has worked incredibly hard to press this idea into the center of political debate. And the place that I was most grateful as you'll hear in the beginning of this podcast. Most grateful that he was able to succeed in convincing someone was his work with Senator Bernie Sanders. Roe was the co-chairman of Bernie Sanders presidential campaign. And in that role, he succeeded in getting Bernie to see why vouchers would be such an important part of any solution to the corrupting influence of money and politics. And you'll hear a little bit in this discussion about how he got Bernie to see that, but that he succeeded in that. And my view is one of the most important contributions he's made. Because now we can begin to see how across the range of positions in the Democratic Party, and let's hope also in the Republican Party, there's a recognition of how we could fund campaigns differently in a way that would radically change the way politics works. So I'm eager to welcome my friend and a longtime collaborator, Roghana. Thank you so much for talking to us. As you know, we've been talking on this podcast about the question of reform and the urgent need to find reform inside of our political system. You, as co-chairman of Bernie's campaign, We're quite successful in getting Senator Sanders to focus enormous energy on the question of reform. I wonder how do you find Democrats when you raise this question of reform in particular, the way we fund campaigns? How do you find them, especially ones who've been around DC forever?
